title: TOK M27 Essay Prompt 5: Simplicity Explained
summary: Learn to answer TOK M27 Essay Prompt 5 on simplicity with two AOKs, a qualified thesis, examples, counterclaims, and clear structure.

### TOK M27 Essay Prompt 5: How to Discuss Simplicity


> **In the production of knowledge, when choosing one explanation over another, to what extent should simplicity be prioritized? Discuss with reference to two areas of knowledge.**


This TOK essay prompt asks whether a simpler explanation should usually be preferred when several explanations compete. A strong response will not claim that simplicity is always best or that it never matters. Instead, it should evaluate when simplicity improves an explanation, when it hides important complexity, and how different **areas of knowledge** judge that trade-off.


This guide explains the key terms, suggests effective AOK combinations, develops claims and counterclaims, and gives you a practical structure. The May 2027 prescribed titles should be checked against the official IB release through your school, so treat the wording above as the prompt assigned to you rather than assuming every online list is official.


### What the TOK prompt is really asking


The phrase **“choosing one explanation over another”** is central. The question is not simply whether simple explanations are attractive. It asks what standards should guide a decision between competing explanations that attempt to account for the same evidence or phenomenon.


The title also specifies **“in the production of knowledge.”** This moves the essay beyond personal preference. You need to discuss how researchers, historians, artists, or communities decide that one explanation is more convincing, useful, or justified.


Finally, **“to what extent”** requires a qualified judgement. Identify circumstances in which simplicity deserves significant weight, then examine cases where other values are more important, such as evidence, explanatory scope, predictive accuracy, ethical responsibility, or attention to individual cases.


A useful starting position is:


> When two explanations are similarly well supported, simplicity should usually be preferred because it reduces unnecessary assumptions. However, simplicity should not outweigh evidence, accuracy, explanatory scope, or the complexity of the phenomenon being explained.


Your examples should determine how far you ultimately agree with this position.


### Define simplicity carefully


In ordinary language, a simple explanation is short or easy to understand. In TOK, a more useful definition is **parsimony** : preferring an explanation that accounts for the relevant evidence while making fewer unnecessary assumptions.


This idea is often associated with **Occam’s razor** , but Occam’s razor is not a rule saying that the shortest explanation must be true. It is a methodological preference. If two explanations explain the evidence equally well, the one with fewer unsupported assumptions may be more defensible because it is easier to test, communicate, and revise.


Simplicity can refer to several features:


- **Structural simplicity:** fewer entities, variables, or assumptions.
- **Mathematical simplicity:** an economical model or equation.
- **Communicative simplicity:** an explanation that is easy to understand.
- **Causal simplicity:** a small number of proposed causes.
- **Practical simplicity:** an explanation that supports decisions or predictions.


These forms can conflict. A simple classroom model may be easy to understand but scientifically incomplete. An equation may be concise while representing a highly complex theory. A public explanation may communicate effectively but distort uncertainty. This distinction matters because an explanation can be simple in presentation without being simple in structure, while a complicated explanation may be more accurate when the phenomenon involves many interacting factors.


### Choosing two areas of knowledge


The prompt does not prescribe particular AOKs. Choose areas where the role of simplicity genuinely differs rather than selecting two areas only because you already know their content.


### Natural sciences and human sciences


This is an effective combination because both AOKs use explanations, models, and evidence, but they often deal with different kinds of complexity. In the **natural sciences** , simplicity can support general laws, prediction, and testability. A model that explains many observations with few assumptions is often valuable, although natural phenomena may require complicated models because variables interact and measurements contain uncertainty.


In the **human sciences** , simplicity can make theories understandable and useful, but human behaviour is shaped by culture, history, institutions, identity, and interpretation. Reducing behaviour to one cause may produce a neat explanation while ignoring factors that matter most.


### Mathematics and natural sciences


Mathematics offers a useful contrast because proof and logical structure play a central role. A simpler proof may be preferred for elegance, accessibility, or generalizability, but a longer proof is not automatically less valid.


The natural sciences evaluate explanations partly through empirical evidence and predictive success. This pairing allows you to compare simplicity as an aesthetic or methodological value in mathematics with simplicity as a model-selection principle in science. The best pair is the one for which you can explain specific examples rather than merely naming famous theories.


### Natural sciences: why simplicity can be powerful


A strong claim is that simplicity should be prioritized when competing explanations have comparable empirical support. A less complicated model may require fewer assumptions, be easier to test, and produce clearer predictions. It can also help scientists identify important variables instead of adding explanations whenever an observation is inconvenient.


For example, **germ theory** offered a more powerful explanation for many infectious diseases than vague accounts based on environmental imbalance or “bad air.” Its strength was not simply that it was easier to describe. It connected specific diseases to microorganisms and generated testable consequences, including the importance of hygiene and sterilization.


The TOK point is that simplicity is valuable when linked to **explanatory and predictive power** . A simple explanation that fails to predict observations is not preferable merely because it is elegant. Simplicity helps choose between explanations only when it operates alongside evidence and testing.


A counterclaim is that scientific explanations sometimes need to become more complex because the world itself is complex. Climate models, for instance, must account for interacting atmospheric, oceanic, biological, and human systems. A deliberately simple model may clarify one relationship, but it can become misleading if used to represent the entire climate system.


Scientists may therefore use a simple model for teaching or initial investigation, while prioritizing greater complexity when omitting variables materially changes the conclusion. This shows that “simple” and “better” are not synonyms.


### Human sciences: usefulness and danger


In the human sciences, simplicity can make explanations more usable. A framework with a small number of clearly defined variables may allow researchers to compare cases, communicate findings, and design studies. Public policy also requires some simplification because decision-makers cannot act on an explanation containing every possible social influence.


An economic model may begin with assumptions about incentives and rational decision-making. These assumptions simplify human behaviour, but they can still help researchers identify patterns and generate predictions. A simplified model is not necessarily claiming that every person behaves identically. It may be a controlled starting point for investigating one relationship.


This supports the argument that simplicity can improve **clarity and operational usefulness** . Without abstraction, the human sciences might produce detailed descriptions of individual cases without developing explanations that can be compared or applied more widely.


However, human behaviour is often context-dependent. A simple explanation may appear objective while excluding variables that are difficult to measure, such as power, language, cultural expectations, social identity, or historical conditions.


Consider the use of a single average to describe a population. An average can simplify a large dataset and reveal a broad pattern, but it may conceal major differences between groups. If a policy is based only on the average result, it may benefit some people while failing others. The explanation is computationally simple but socially inadequate.


Psychological explanations can face a similar problem when complex behaviour is attributed to one trait or mechanism. In this AOK, simplicity should be balanced against **representativeness, cultural sensitivity, and the consequences of applying the explanation** .


### Comparing the two AOKs


Do not write two disconnected mini-essays. Compare what simplicity does in each AOK and why the standards differ.


In the natural sciences, simplicity often helps researchers construct models that are testable and predictive. Complexity is justified when it increases empirical accuracy or captures important interactions. In the human sciences, simplicity can improve comparison and communication, but it carries a greater risk of removing the social context that gives behaviour its meaning.


This does not mean that natural science is objective and human science is subjective. Both AOKs use methods to control bias and evaluate evidence. The difference is that human beings are simultaneously the objects of study and interpreters of knowledge, making context and reflexivity especially important.


A comparative thesis could be:


> Simplicity should be prioritized as a starting point when it preserves the evidence and makes an explanation testable or useful. However, it should be subordinated to accuracy and contextual adequacy when removing complexity changes the phenomenon being explained. Simplicity is therefore a conditional methodological virtue rather than a universal measure of knowledge.


### Suggested essay structure


### Introduction


Define simplicity as parsimony rather than ease of understanding. Introduce the two AOKs and state a qualified thesis about when simplicity should be prioritized.


### Claims and counterclaims


For the natural sciences, present an example in which a relatively simple explanation improved prediction, testing, or unification. Then show how a more complex model became necessary because the simpler explanation excluded relevant variables. Explain whether the additional complexity improved knowledge or merely made the explanation harder to use.


For the human sciences, use an example in which simplification made behaviour measurable, comparable, or useful for policy. Clarify what the model explains and what it leaves out. Then show how ignoring culture, context, or differences between groups weakened the explanation and created practical or ethical consequences.


### Conclusion


Answer “to what extent” directly. State the conditions under which simplicity should be prioritized and identify the standards that must override it, such as evidence, predictive accuracy, explanatory scope, and contextual adequacy.


For planning support, use a[TOK essay planning guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/tok-may-2026-essay-prescribed-titles-complete-guide-for-students) , review[the five TOK Areas of Knowledge](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/overview-of-the-five-areas-of-knowledge-in-tok) , and practise connecting broad wording to AOKs and themes with[RevisionDojo’s TOK resources](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/linking-tok-may-2026-titles-to-areas-of-knowledge-and-themes) .


### Common mistakes and revision advice


Avoid treating Occam’s razor as proof. It can guide selection, but it does not establish truth. Also avoid defining simple as easy, assuming complexity is automatically better, or using examples descriptively without explaining how they change your judgement.


After writing each paragraph, ask: **What explanation is being preferred? Why is it simpler? What might be lost by choosing it?** These questions help you move from description to evaluation.


Underline every sentence that connects back to the title. If a paragraph discusses evidence or models without explaining whether simplicity should be prioritized, it needs a clearer analytical link. Test your thesis by reversing it: if you claim simplicity usually matters, identify a case where it fails; if you claim accuracy always matters more, explain why researchers still use idealized models.


The IB describes the TOK essay as a formal response to a prescribed title and assesses whether the student provides a clear, coherent, and critical exploration of that title. Polished vocabulary cannot compensate for weak evaluation. Specific examples, explicit reasoning, and sustained focus on the question matter more than mentioning famous theories.


RevisionDojo’s[IB TOK Essay Grader](https://www.revisiondojo.com/grader/rubric/tok-essay) can help you check focus, examples, and evaluation. Use feedback as a revision aid, not as a replacement for your reasoning or teacher’s guidance.


### Conclusion


For TOK M27 Essay Prompt 5, simplicity should be presented as a valuable but conditional standard. It can reduce unnecessary assumptions, improve testability, support communication, and make models useful. Nevertheless, it becomes weak when it sacrifices evidence, predictive accuracy, explanatory scope, context, or ethical responsibility.


The most convincing essay will compare this balance in two AOKs and reach a precise judgement. Start with natural sciences and human sciences if you can support both with specific examples, then explain not merely that simplicity matters, but **when it should be allowed to matter most** .
